newsitem.title: TAIWAN: FEATURE-Taiwanese still rue island's 1945 handover.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Taiwanese still rue island's 1945 handover.

text.p: Hong Kong's negotiated transfer to China awakens bitter memories in older Taiwanese who still recall their island's traumatic handover to the mainland after 50 years of Japanese colonial rule.

Both handovers were clinched behind closed doors without local consent, but Hong Kong people have benefited from intense media coverage since British and Chinese negotiators sat down in the early 1980s to seal the territory's fate.
China's corrupt, decaying Qing dynasty ceded Taiwan to Japan through the 1895 Treaty of Shimonoseki as a war indemnity.
Following its defeat in World War II, Japan handed Taiwan back to the Chinese Nationalists.

Word of the Taiwan people's destiny simply rained down from the sky. "I first knew about it from some pamphlets dropped by U.S. aircraft," 74-year-old retired civil engineer Cheng Ah-lai told Reuters in an interview.

"The pamphlets -- written in Japanese -- vaguely mentioned something about the Cairo Declaration and that Taiwan would be returned to China," recalled Cheng, who was a municipal worker in the southern port city of Kaohsiung.
"It wasn't very clear at the time what would happen next. We were too afraid to ask," Cheng added.
A FATE SEALED FAR AWAY

Japan took two decades to crush resistance during its initial colonial period, executing 10,000 people, and spent the rest of its 50-year occupation remoulding Taiwan in its own image, obliging Taiwanese to take Japanese names, undergo Japanese education and live Japanese lives.
Many Taiwanese had come to see themselves as Japanese.

But wrenching change was to come again as Taiwan's post-war fate was sealed far away in Cairo, where Chinese Nationalist leader Chiang Kai-shek met in 1943 with U.S. President Franklin Roosevelt and British Prime Minister Winston Churchill.
The December 1 Cairo declaration demanded Japan's surrender and the return of its occupied lands.
On October 25, 1945, Taiwan was handed by the allied victors to Chiang's tottering Nationalist government.
Chang Lung-hui, then a young surgeon practising in Taiwan's central Taichung county, remembers the handover clearly.
"We had been treated like second-class citizens under Japanese colonial rule," the 77-year-old Chang said.
"Taiwan was an orphan brought up by an adoptive parent," Chang said. "We were delighted that finally it could reunite with its biological parent."
But the dream of a happy reunion evaporated quickly.
NATIONALIST CHINESE TROOPS SHOCK LOCALS
Chiang's Nationalists fled to Taiwan after a 1949 civil war defeat at the hands of the Communists led to the establishment of the People's Republic of China on the mainland.
The arrival of Nationalist troops led by administrator Chen Yi was a crushing disappointment.
"It was such a shock. The Chinese soldiers were poorly trained and undisciplined. They dressed sloppily and showed no respect to local people," Cheng said.
"I remembered I said to myself -- they would be worse than the Japanese."
Chang recalled the same unpleasant memory.
"I was disappointed from the very instant I saw the arrival of the Chinese Nationalist troops," Chang said.
"Let's put it this way. The defeated Japanese soldiers waiting to be deported were much more disciplined than the victorious Chinese soldiers," Chang said.
"The Chinese soldiers were like a bunch of bandits -- they robbed and stole from local people after they came," he said. "I began to miss the days under Japanese rule."
TENSION COMES TO A HEAD
Mounting anti-government sentiment among Taiwanese exploded in 1947 when Chiang authorised the suppression of opposition to Chinese rule. The crackdown escalated into a bloodbath.
The massacre of some 18,000 people in the suppression of anti-Nationalist riots is known universally on Taiwan simply as "228" due to its February 28 beginning.
To this day, though the Nationalists now hold power through free elections, some Taiwanese still regard them as unwelcome interlopers who occupy their island against their will.
"I don't consider myself Chinese or Japanese. The fate of Taiwan was pre-determined by other people, not us," Cheng said.
"If you ask me, I want to be a Taiwanese."
Cheng said Hong Kong's handover reminded him of Taiwan's own dark past and voiced pessimism about the territory's future.
"I am afraid we will see the replay of the 228 incident in Hong Kong in the near future," he said.
